analysis.one_liner: Taxes stock, futures, and swap trades on Wall Street to fund job creation and cut deficits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote; it sat in the Ways and Means, Rules, and Budget committees until the two-year Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a small tax on each Wall Street trade: 0.25% on stock trades and 0.02% on futures, swaps, and credit default swaps. Sponsors estimated it would raise about $150 billion a year. Half would go into a 'Job Creation Reserve' to pay for transportation and job programs, and half would reduce the federal deficit. Retirement accounts, health savings accounts, college savings accounts, and mutual fund shares would be exempt, and households would get a credit covering the tax on their first $100,000 of stock trades each year.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who would gain from the funded transportation and job-creation programs, ordinary retirement savers whose accounts are exempt from the tax, and taxpayers generally through the deficit reduction half.

how_it_helps.text: Half the revenue would be held in a Job Creation Reserve to pay for transportation projects and job-creation legislation that must fund jobs paying at least the median wage and support manufacturing jobs.
The other half would reduce the federal deficit, which the bill's findings put at $1.4 trillion for 2009.

Retirement accounts, health savings accounts, education accounts, and mutual fund investments would be completely exempt, and each purchaser would get a credit of up to $250 ($500 joint) against the tax, so small investors' first $100,000 of stock trades per year would effectively be shielded.

analysis.who_pays: Investment banks, hedge funds, high-frequency trading firms, and other large financial traders who would pay the tax on every qualifying transaction, plus taxable individual investors who trade actively beyond the $250 credit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wall Street trading firms and banks

drawbacks.text: The tax would hit taxable brokerage accounts, not just Wall Street firms: only retirement, health savings, education, and mutual fund accounts are exempt, and the credit shields at most $250 ($500 joint) per year, so active individual traders beyond that would pay directly.

A per-trade tax can push some trading to foreign exchanges or reduce market liquidity, and the $150 billion annual estimate is a sponsor figure rather than an independent estimate, so actual revenue could fall short.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is aimed at ordinary households: the accounts most Americans use are exempt and a per-household credit covers the tax on up to $100,000 of stock purchases, leaving the burden on high-volume traders. The main honest concern is leakage — high-frequency trading and derivatives business could move offshore, shrinking the revenue — and the revenue estimate was not independently verified.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three committees but never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 3, 2009, and referred the same day to the Committees on Ways and Means, Rules, and Budget.
That referral was the last action of any kind; the bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
The bill drew 32 Democratic cosponsors in the House and no recorded Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wall Street trading firms and banks, which never faced the tax; no job-creation or deficit-reduction revenue was ever raised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wall Street firms that avoided the tax

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its case that Wall Street should fund job creation and deficit reduction after the financial bailout.

for.name: 32 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all recorded cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Chair of the committee with jurisdiction over the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup in the two years after referral, leaving it without a path to the floor.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker's office and Democratic majority leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor at any point in the 111th Congress.

against.name: Financial services industry
against.role: Banks, hedge funds, and high-frequency trading firms
against.what_they_did: Opposed securities transaction taxes during the post-bailout period as the industry lobbied against new levies on trading.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 House supporters (the sponsor plus 32 cosponsors) were Democrats, and the bill drew no Republican cosponsors; no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would tax every stock, futures, swap, and credit default swap transaction they execute in the U.S., cutting directly into high-volume trading profits. Avoiding the tax was worth up to an estimated $150 billion a year in revenue that instead went unraised.
A 0.02% tax on each futures, swap, and credit default swap trade is small per trade but large at machine-trading volume, so these firms had the most to lose from any version of the tax.

industries.industry: Mutual fund companies and retirement savers
industries.note: Fund shares and retirement, health savings, and education accounts are expressly exempt, so the bill's structure shields ordinary savers and the fund industry's retail channel from the tax while leaving it on wholesale trading.
